title: Python setup, notebooks and the first program
summary: Set up Python, run your first notebook cell, and write a program that stores and prints information.
objectives: Check that Python is installed and working
Run code cells and text cells in a notebook
Store a value in a variable with =

question.prompt: Which command prints the version of Python installed on your computer?
question.explanation_correct: `python --version` prints the installed version. On macOS and Linux you may need `python3 --version`.
question.explanation_incorrect: Not quite. `python -v` turns on verbose mode, which traces every import. The command that prints the version is `python --version`.

question.prompt: Which statement about notebook cells is true?

options.text: Each cell can be run on its own, and all cells share the same variables while the kernel is running
Every cell has its own separate set of variables
Cells run automatically from top to bottom whenever you open the notebook

question.explanation_correct: Cells share one kernel, so a variable created in one cell can be used by any cell you run afterwards.
question.explanation_incorrect: Not quite. Cells are separate to run but share the same kernel, so variables carry over. You choose when each cell runs.

question.prompt: After running `price = 20` and then `price = price + 5`, what does `print(price)` show?
question.explanation_correct: Python works out the right side first using the old value (20 + 5), then stores 25 back under `price`.
question.explanation_incorrect: Not quite. The second line reads the old value of `price`, adds 5, and stores the answer back, so `price` is now 25.

segments.title: What you will do today
segments.body:
## What you will do today

By the end of this lecture you will have Python running, you will know how a notebook works, and you will have written and submitted your first program.

- Set up Python and check that it works
- Run code and text in a notebook
- Store information in a variable and show it with `print()`

The lecture has three short readings, two knowledge checks, one coding lab and a short exit check. Leave whenever you need to; you resume where you stopped.

Knowledge checks show you how you are doing. The lab and the exit check decide whether the lecture is complete. In the lab you can try as often as you like and your best score is the one that counts.

segments.title: Set up Python
segments.body:
## Two ways to start

You need Python 3 to run the code in this course. Pick one route.

**On your own computer.** Download Python 3.12 or newer from python.org and run the installer. On Windows, tick *Add python.exe to PATH* before you click Install.

**In your browser.** If you cannot install software, use a hosted notebook service such as Google Colab. Python is already installed there.

## Check that it works

Open a terminal (Command Prompt or PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on macOS and Linux) and run:

```
python --version
```

You should see something like `Python 3.12.4`. On macOS and Linux the command is often `python3 --version`.

If the terminal says the command was not found, Python is installed but your computer cannot find it yet. Close the terminal, open a new one and try again. If it still fails on Windows, run the installer again, choose *Modify*, and tick the PATH option.

segments.title: Notebooks and cells
segments.body:
## What a notebook is

A notebook is a document that mixes code, the output of that code, and text. People use notebooks because you can run a small piece, look at the result, and change your mind.

## Cells

A notebook is made of cells. You will use two kinds:

- **Code cells** hold Python. When you run one, its output appears directly beneath it.
- **Text cells** (Markdown) hold notes and headings. They do not run as code.

To run the selected cell, press `Shift + Enter`. The notebook runs it and moves to the next cell.

## The kernel remembers

Behind the notebook is a running Python process called the kernel. Every cell shares it. If one cell contains:

```
x = 5
```

then a later cell containing `print(x)` shows `5`, for as long as the kernel is running.

Order matters. Cells run in the order you run them, which is not always top to bottom. When a result looks wrong, restart the kernel and run every cell from the top.

segments.title: Variables and print()
segments.body:
## Your first program

A program is a list of instructions that Python follows one line at a time. Here is a complete one:

```
student_name = "Aarav"
print(student_name)
```

Running it shows:

```
Aarav
```

## What each line does

- `student_name = "Aarav"` creates a **variable**. The name goes on the left, the value on the right, and `=` stores the value under that name. Text must be wrapped in quotes.
- `print(student_name)` shows the value on screen. There are no quotes around `student_name`, because you are printing what the variable holds, not the word itself.

## Changing a variable

A variable can be given a new value at any time. Python works out the right-hand side first:

```
price = 20
price = price + 5
print(price)
```

This prints `25`. Python reads `price + 5` using the old value (20), then stores the answer back under `price`.

## Joining text with +

Two pieces of text can be joined with `+`:

```
name = "Aarav"
greeting = "Hello, my name is " + name
print(greeting)
```

This prints `Hello, my name is Aarav`. Notice the space at the end of `"Hello, my name is "`. Without it the words run together.

## Reading an error message

Programs do not always work the first time. Try this:

```
name = "Aarav"
print(nme)
```

Python stops and shows:

```
NameError: name 'nme' is not defined
```

Read it from the end. Python looked for a variable called `nme` and did not find one, because the variable is called `name`. The message also tells you the line number. Fix the spelling, run again, and it works. Reading an error calmly and fixing it is a skill you will use every day.

## Common mistakes

- `print("student_name")` with quotes prints the words, not the value.
- A misspelled variable name causes a `NameError`. Check the spelling against the line where you created the variable.
- One `=` stores a value. Two, `==`, compare two values; you will use that later.
- A missing closing quote or bracket causes a `SyntaxError`. Python tells you which line.

In the lab you will write hello.py: a greeting with your own name and two facts about you. One line is broken on purpose so that you can read the error and fix it yourself.

lab.title: hello.py: a greeting and a fixed typo
lab.objective: Write hello.py: a greeting with your own name and two facts, and fix a broken line by reading its error message.
lab.instructions: Write your first program, hello.py. Store your name in name and build greeting from the words Hello, my name is and your name. The print line in step 3 has a typo on purpose: press Run, read the NameError, then fix it. Store two facts about yourself in fact_1 and fact_2 and print them, one per line, after the greeting. Finally, store the corrected print line from step 3 as text between quotes in fixed_line.
lab.constraints: Keep the variable names name, greeting, fact_1, fact_2 and fixed_line. Print each line with print(). No input() and no imports.
lab.starter_code:
# hello.py - my first program

# 1. Put your own name between the quotes
name = ""

# 2. Build the greeting: the words "Hello, my name is " followed by your name
greeting = "Hello, my name is " + name

# 3. Print the greeting.
#    This line has a typo on purpose. Press Run, read the NameError, then fix it.
print(greting)

# 4. Store two facts about yourself, in quotes, for example "I am 13 years old"
fact_1 = ""
fact_2 = ""

# 5. Print fact_1, then fact_2, each on its own line


# 6. Write the corrected line from step 3 as text between the quotes
fixed_line = ""
hints: Press Run first. The NameError tells you the line number and the name Python cannot find. Compare that name with the variable you created in step 2.
The variable is spelled greeting, so the print line must be print(greeting). Then fill in name, fact_1 and fact_2, and print both facts with print(fact_1) and print(fact_2).
The last step is text, not code: fixed_line = "print(greeting)" is the corrected line written between quotes.

visible_examples.code:
city = "Pune"
message = "I live in " + city
print(message)

pet = "a dog"
print("I have " + pet)
print("It is brown")
visible_examples.expected_output:
I have a dog
It is brown

success_criteria: Your program runs without an error and prints something
name holds your name (text, not empty)
A printed line reads Hello, my name is followed by your name
fact_1 and fact_2 each hold a different fact (text, not empty)
At least three lines are printed: the greeting and the two facts
fixed_line holds the corrected print line from step 3, as text

lab.solution:

greeting = "Hello, my name is " + name
print(greeting)
fact_1 = "I am 13 years old"
fact_2 = "I like cricket"

print(fact_2)
